Baby & Child

How to encourage a child in everyday activities

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Your child has left paint on the table but put the lid back on the yellow jar before it dried out. Which part will they hear about? “You put the lid back on. That keeps the paint ready for tomorrow.” There is still a table to wipe. Noticing what helped makes it easier to explain the next job without turning the whole afternoon into a verdict on how tidy your child is.

Name the action while it is still fresh

Think of what another person could have seen or heard. A child handed back a marker, moved their cup before it tipped or waited until a friend finished speaking. Name that detail in a natural voice. If it helps, explain the effect: “You moved the cup. Now there’s room for the book.” The child can connect the words to something they actually did.

Encouragement can be quiet. Some children like a cheerful high five, others dislike being singled out in front of people. A smile or a few private words may work better. Give attention to things you enjoy together as well. A child should be able to bring you a picture simply because they want you to see it.

Notice an approach the child can use again

For homework, look for an action that moved the child forward. “You put a dot next to the question you want to ask tomorrow” gives them a way to handle the next hard problem. If the method has not helped, ask which part feels confusing and whether an example or a break would help. Praising effort over and over will not make an unclear instruction easier.

Researchers who observed 53 families when the children were 14 to 38 months old found an association five years later. Children who heard a higher proportion of praise about what they did tended to see more potential for skills to develop at ages seven to eight. The study observed families as they were. It cannot establish that a certain phrase caused a particular child’s beliefs.

Make the next step possible

Before asking a preschooler to put painting things away, check whether they can reach the shelf and tell where everything goes. Show one step and leave them a real part to do. A small job with an obvious finish gives you something honest to recognise. If a task routinely ends in an argument, ask what is getting in the way. Listen to the answer before giving another instruction.

Choose the few limits that matter and give a short, positive direction the child can follow. Put breakable items out of reach before inviting them to help. Keep the promises you make and model your own request: if you ask for a quiet voice, lower yours too. Acknowledge frustration while holding a reasonable boundary. A playful clean-up sound can lighten the job if your child enjoys it.

At the table, leave appetite out of the score

A family meal is an opportunity to model eating a variety of foods and share a routine. Offer food appropriate for the child and let them decide how much to eat. Saying “You carried the napkins to the table” notices a contribution without making approval depend on eating another bite. Avoid using dessert, affection or praise as the price for clearing the plate.

If eating is difficult, look at what happens rather than adding more encouragement. A child who seems to have pain when eating, often chokes or is losing weight needs advice from a healthcare professional. For ordinary reluctance, a calm opportunity to see the food again on another day keeps the door open.

When the words fall flat

A child may shrug at praise or disagree with it. If they say a drawing went badly, ask which part they mean. You might say, “I see the blue stripe ended up wider than you wanted. What would you like to do with it?” Listening gives them a say in the conversation and keeps exaggeration out of it.

Try noticing one specific action in a familiar routine this week. If the child still struggles, change the task, the timing or the help available. Invite them to show you what would make tomorrow easier. Specific encouragement is one way to support learning, alongside clear teaching, rest and help when something is genuinely hard.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Choose feedback that describes an observable action.

If encouragement is not helping, check understanding and change the support.

Keep food, affection and connection available without requiring a child to earn them.

How BeMama can help

BeMama uses the lid of a paint jar to show how a parent can recognise a helpful step and still guide a child through the rest of a task.

When to seek help

Ask a healthcare professional about pain with eating, frequent choking or concerns about weight or growth. If a child is choking and cannot breathe, seek emergency help immediately.

Sources and further reading

  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Using specific praise with toddlers and preschoolers
  • Gunderson and colleagues, Child Development — Parent praise in the early years and later beliefs about learning
  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Helping a child try foods without pressure or bribes

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Describe what the child did and, when useful, what difference it made.
  • Name a strategy the child can try again during homework.
  • Make the task reachable and model what you are asking for.
  • At meals, notice participation while letting the child decide how much to eat.

Frequently asked questions

How can I encourage my child at meals?

Offer suitable foods and share the meal when you can. Invite the child to help with a small job, such as setting out spoons. Let them decide how much to eat and avoid tying approval or a treat to finishing the plate.

What can I say when my child does something helpful?

Pick a detail they can recognise. “You held the door until the buggy was through” tells them more than a broad compliment. If they prefer little fuss, a simple thank-you can be enough.

How do I encourage a child to begin homework?

Check that they know the task and have what they need. Agree on a first step and notice it when it happens. If getting started remains hard, ask what is confusing and speak with the teacher about work that consistently feels out of reach.

What helps a useful behaviour happen again?

Make the action possible, demonstrate it, and notice it soon after it happens. A reachable hook for a coat may do more than another reminder. Keep expectations realistic and give your child another chance to practise.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
